# 2 Kings Chapter 20 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 241v–242r | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_020_page_481.jpg, 2KI_020_page_482.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** In those days Hezekiah became ill and was at the point of death. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, "Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die; you shall not recover."

**2** Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD:

**3** "Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.

**4** Before Isaiah had gone out of the middle court, the word of the LORD came to him:

**5** "Turn back and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will heal you. On the third day you shall go up to the house of the LORD.

**6** I will add fifteen years to your life. I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."

**7** Then Isaiah said, "Bring a cake of figs." They brought it and laid it on the boil, and he recovered.

**8** Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "What shall be the sign that the LORD will heal me, and that I shall go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?"

**9** Isaiah said, "This is the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do what he has spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?"

**10** Hezekiah answered, "It is easy for the shadow to lengthen ten steps. Rather let the shadow go back ten steps."

**11** And Isaiah the prophet called to the LORD, and he brought the shadow back ten steps, by which it had gone down on the steps of Ahaz.

**12** At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill.

**13** Hezekiah welcomed them and showed them all his treasure house — the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his armory, and everything that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.

**14** Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah and said to him, "What did these men say? And where did they come from?" Hezekiah said, "They have come from a far country, from Babylon."

**15** He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."

**16** Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD:

**17** Behold, the days are coming when all that is in your house, and all that your fathers have stored up to this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.

**18** And some of your own sons, who will be born to you, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."

**19** Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "Is it not so, if there will be peace and security in my days?"

**20** The rest of the deeds of Hezekiah, all his might, and how he made the pool and the conduit and brought water into the city — are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?

**21** And Hezekiah lay down with his fathers, and Manasseh his son reigned in his place.

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Chapter 20 is the decline of Hezekiah — the great king brought low not by enemies but by illness, vanity, and shortsightedness. The first movement (vv.1-11) is a story of prayer and reversal: a death sentence undone, time itself reversed on the stairway of Ahaz. It is one of the Bible's most powerful testimonies to the efficacy of prayer. The second movement (vv.12-19) is the chapter's tragedy: Hezekiah, freshly healed, receives Babylonian envoys and shows them everything. The narrator's emphasis — "there was nothing he did not show them" — signals that this is not hospitality but hubris. Isaiah's prophecy (vv.17-18) transforms the Babylonians from visitors to future conquerors: everything Hezekiah showed them, they will take. His descendants will serve as eunuchs in the palace he boasted of. Hezekiah's final words (v.19) are the chapter's moral test: does he accept the judgment with faith, or is he simply relieved it will not happen in his lifetime? The narrator refuses to tell us. But the mention of Manasseh — the worst king in Judah's history — as Hezekiah's successor casts a long shadow. The seeds of exile are planted in the golden age.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.1 — "Command your house" vs. "Set your house in order" vs. "Put your affairs in order"
- **EMET:** "Command [tsav] your-house [le-veytekha]"
- **LOGOS:** "Set your house in order"
- **PNEUMA:** "Put your affairs in order"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "Set your house in order" — *tsav le-veytekha* literally means "command your house," but the English idiom "set your house in order" perfectly captures the meaning (making a will, arranging succession) and is the traditional rendering.

### V.3 — "in truth" vs. "in faithfulness" vs. "faithfully"
- **EMET:** "in-truth [be-emet]"
- **LOGOS:** "in faithfulness"
- **PNEUMA:** "faithfully"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "in faithfulness" — *emet* means truth, faithfulness, reliability. "Faithfulness" captures the covenantal dimension better than the more abstract "truth," while retaining a noun form closer to the Hebrew.

### V.7 — "cake of figs" vs. "paste of figs"
- **EMET:** "a-cake of-figs [develat te'enim]"
- **LOGOS:** "a cake of figs"
- **PNEUMA:** "a paste of figs"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "a cake of figs" — *develah* is a pressed fig cake, not a paste. "Cake" accurately describes the form.

### V.13 — "listened to them" vs. "welcomed them" vs. "was delighted"
- **EMET:** "And-listened [vayishma'] to-them"
- **LOGOS:** "welcomed them"
- **PNEUMA:** "was delighted by the attention"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "welcomed them" — *shama'* here means to listen favorably, to receive. "Welcomed" captures the social context. PNEUMA's "was delighted by the attention" adds a psychological interpretation not explicit in the Hebrew.

### V.19 — Hezekiah's motive: ambiguous vs. interpreted
- **EMET:** "Is-it-not [ha-lo'] [so], if [im] peace [shalom] and-truth [emet] shall-be [yihyeh] in-my-days?"
- **LOGOS:** "For he thought, 'Is it not so, if there will be peace and security in my days?'"
- **PNEUMA:** "At least there will be peace and stability during my lifetime."
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "For he thought, 'Is it not so, if there will be peace and security in my days?'" — LOGOS preserves the Hebrew's ambiguity by framing it as an interior thought with a question. PNEUMA collapses the ambiguity into a declarative statement of selfish relief, which is one valid reading but not the only one.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
